note_tweet.text:
Much of the economic data we use to understand the world, such as the incomes people receive, is recorded in the local currencies of each country. On their own, numbers in local currencies tell us nothing about how they compare. One obvious approach would be to convert them into a common currency using market exchange rates. But this doesn’t give us the comparison we often look for: what money can actually buy in different countries. This is because the cost of living varies a lot across countries.

International dollars are a hypothetical currency that aims to have the same purchasing power everywhere. They are adjusted for differences in living costs across countries and price changes over time. Wherever it is “spent”, one international dollar buys the same goods and services as one US dollar would in the United States.

Making incomes comparable across countries matters especially for our understanding of global inequality. Using market dollars — local currencies converted to US dollars using market exchange rates — to compare incomes across countries understates people’s real income in countries where local prices are often much lower than in the US.

Take India, for example. Its gross domestic product (GDP) per capita is almost 30 times lower than that of the US in market dollars. But when we adjust for differences in living costs, the gap shrinks to about eight times lower. For Burkina Faso, the difference is even starker: its GDP per capita is 83 times lower than that of the US in market dollars, and 30 times lower after adjusting for differences in living costs. Global inequality remains large, even after accounting for what people can buy locally.

note_tweet.text:
🚨 BIG NEWS: $NBIS NEBIUS IMPROVES AI TRAINING THROUGHPUT ON 192 NVIDIA B300 GPUs WITHOUT ADDING A SINGLE GPU.

This is a pretty bug technical update from Nebius.

Nebius tested NUMA-aware process affinity on a DeepSeek V3 pretraining workload running across 192 NVIDIA B300 GPUs using Megatron Bridge on its managed Kubernetes platform.

The results? Mean training step time decreased by 1.11%, while model throughput per GPU increased by 1.13%.

Now, 1.13% might not sound impressive initially. But when you're operating thousands of expensive GPUs, even a small improvement in utilization can have meaningful economic value.

Modern GPU servers have multiple CPU sockets and NUMA domains. Each CPU has faster access to its local memory and PCIe connected devices. When training processes get scheduled across the wrong NUMA domains, they can introduce unnecessary memory traffic, latency and communication overhead.

Nebius tested exclusive NUMA binding, which keeps processes closer to their local CPU, memory and GPU resources.

The important part is that they're improving performance through infrastructure level optimization rather than buying additional compute.

Imagine a hypothetical 100,000 GPU deployment achieving the same 1.13% throughput improvement. That's roughly the training throughput equivalent of adding 1,130 GPUs, assuming the improvement scales consistently.

Of course, this benchmark doesn't prove the same gains will hold across every model, cluster or workload.

Nebius is operating in a market where GPUs are extremely expensive, power availability is constrained and customers care about how quickly they can train models.

If Nebius can consistently extract more useful compute from the same hardware, customers can finish training workloads faster while Nebius potentially improves the competitiveness and economics of its cloud platform.

This wasn't a synthetic GPU benchmark. Nebius used a DeepSeek V3 pretraining workload with Megatron Bridge, which makes the result more relevant to actual large model training.

This is what separates simply renting NVIDIA GPUs from building a serious AI cloud platform.

Anybody with enough capital can purchase GPUs. Getting those GPUs to operate efficiently across CPU topology, memory, networking, containers and distributed training software is an entirely different engineering problem.

Nebius is showing that it's paying attention to that layer and as its GPU infrastructure scales, these seemingly small optimizations could become increasingly important to its customers and its own infrastructure economics.

It is true that spending on goods and services creates nominal income, but it increases aggregate real income only to the extent that it leads to an expansion in real production.

It is also true, as an accounting identity, that a government deficit has a counterpart in a net financial surplus outside government, but the identity tells us nothing about the direction of causation. The causal relationship can run in either direction, and the two can reinforce one another.

Finally, although many MMTers are emphatic about the first four propositions, they too often forget the fifth, which may be the most important.
